10.	The full name of this city is Nuestra Señora de X given to it in 1548 by its Spanish founder, Captain Alonso de Mendoza, to commemorate the restoration of peace after a violent civil war among rival conquistadors. The city is famous for its Mercado de las Brujas (Witches’ Market), where Aymara stallholders sell amulets, herbs, and dried llama fetuses to be buried beneath the foundations of new houses as offerings to Pachamama, the Earth Mother. It is also famous for cholita wrestling — indigenous Aymara women in their traditional bowler hats and many-layered pollera skirts performing acrobatic lucha libre to enthusiastic local crowds. The country it serves has the unusual distinction of having two capitals: a smaller white-walled city far to the southeast is the constitutional capital, but it is in this city that the executive branch and the country’s parliament actually sit. Name the city (10 points). ‎<attached: 00137151-PHOTO-2026-04-30-09-24-20.jpg>
La Paz literally means “the peace” — named “our lady of the peace” to mark the peace following a civil war

9.	In 1978, this city was one of the very first two places ever inscribed on the brand-new UNESCO World Heritage list (the other was Kraków in Poland). It was founded by the Spanish in 1534 on the ruins of an Inca city, which had itself been built atop a still-older pre-Inca settlement; it nestles right at the foot of the active stratovolcano Pichincha, whose lower slopes loom directly over the city’s western edge. In August 1809, this city was the site of the “Primer Grito de Independencia” — the first cry for independence in all of Spanish America. About 26 km north of the historic center, a yellow-and-red obelisk called the Mitad del Mundo (“Middle of the World”) marks — with a small but well-known eighteenth-century imprecision — the very imaginary line for which the country itself is named. Name the city (10 points). ‎<attached: 00137160-PHOTO-2026-04-30-09-26-05.jpg>
